claim: Chlamydia trachomatis causes nearly 100 million sexually transmitted infections annually worldwide.
source: C. trachomatis causes nearly 100 million sexually transmitted infections annually worldwide, and if left unchecked leads to various human diseases including infection-induced blindness, pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility and ectopic pregnancy (Aral et al., 2006; Newman et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Aral et al., 2006; Newman et al., 2015).

claim: C. trachomatis infection can lead to infection-induced blindness, pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility and ectopic pregnancy.
source: C. trachomatis causes nearly 100 million sexually transmitted infections annually worldwide, and if left unchecked leads to various human diseases including infection-induced blindness, pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility and ectopic pregnancy (Aral et al., 2006; Newman et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Aral et al., 2006; Newman et al., 2015).

claim: Chlamydial infections can generally be treated with antibiotics.
source: Even though chlamydial infections can generally be treated with antibiotics, persistent infections remain a challenge (Kohlhoff and Hammerschlag, 2015; Mpiga and Ravaoarinoro, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kohlhoff and Hammerschlag, 2015; Mpiga and Ravaoarinoro, 2006).

claim: Persistent chlamydial infections remain a challenge.
source: Even though chlamydial infections can generally be treated with antibiotics, persistent infections remain a challenge (Kohlhoff and Hammerschlag, 2015; Mpiga and Ravaoarinoro, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kohlhoff and Hammerschlag, 2015; Mpiga and Ravaoarinoro, 2006).

claim: All Chlamydiae share a common dimorphic life cycle where bacteria alternate between infectious but non-dividing elementary body (EB) form and non-infectious but replicative reticulate body (RB) form.
source: All Chlamydiae share a common dimorphic life cycle, where the bacteria alternates between the infectious but non-dividing elementary body (EB) form, and the non-infectious but replicative reticulate body (RB) form.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about chlamydial biology.

claim: Following internalization of EBs, bacteria reside in a membrane-bound vacuole termed the inclusion where they convert into RBs and replication occurs over 24–72 hr.
source: Following internalization of EBs through a poorly defined endocytic process, the bacteria reside in a membrane-bound vacuole termed the inclusion, where they convert into RBs and replication occurs over 24–72 hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about chlamydial biology.

claim: Chlamydiae secrete more than fifty different Inc proteins.
source: Chlamydiae secrete more than fifty different Inc proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about chlamydial biology.

claim: Incs possess little sequence similarity but share a common membrane topology with cytoplasmic N- and C-terminal domains, separated by two closely spaced transmembrane regions with a short intra-vacuolar loop.
source: While Incs possess little sequence similarity, they share a common membrane topology with cytoplasmic N- and C-terminal domains, separated by two closely spaced transmembrane regions with a short intra-vacuolar loop (Dehoux et al., 2011; Kostriukova et al., 2008; Li et al., 2008; Lutter et al., 2012; Rockey et al., 2002) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dehoux et al., 2011; Kostriukova et al., 2008; Li et al., 2008; Lutter et al., 2012; Rockey et al., 2002) and Figure 1A.

claim: SNX1, SNX2, SNX5 and SNX6 are recruited to the inclusion membrane in C. trachomatis infected cells.
source: It was previously shown that the sorting nexins SNX1, SNX2, SNX5 and SNX6 are recruited to the inclusion membrane in C. trachomatis infected cells (Aeberhard et al., 2015; Mirrashidi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Aeberhard et al., 2015; Mirrashidi et al., 2015).

claim: Myc-tagged SNX1, SNX2 and SNX5 are recruited to the inclusion membrane in HeLa cells infected with C. trachomatis serovar L2.
source: We first confirmed this for myc-tagged SNX1, SNX2 and SNX5 in HeLa cells infected with C. trachomatis serovar L2 (MOI ~0.5) for 18 hr. All three proteins were recruited to the inclusion membrane as assessed by co-localisation with the inclusion marker mCherry-Rab25 (Figure 1B) (Teo et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and cited literature (Teo et al., 2016).

claim: GFP-tagged SNX1 and SNX5 but not GFP-SNX8 are recruited to inclusion membranes.
source: as were GFP-tagged SNX1 and SNX5 but not the more distantly homologous GFP-SNX8 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment with wortmannin causes loss of SNX proteins from punctate endosomes but not from the inclusion membrane.
source: Interestingly, when infected cells are treated with wortmannin, a pan-specific inhibitor of phosphoinositide-3-kinase (PI3K) activity, we see a loss of the SNX proteins from punctate endosomes, but not from the inclusion membrane (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Video 1.

claim: Specific inhibition of PtdIns3P production by Vps34 using Vps34-IN1 causes loss of SNX proteins from punctate endosomes but not from the inclusion membrane.
source: A similar result is seen for specific inhibition of PtdIns3P production by Vps34 using Vps34-IN1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The C-terminal domain of IncE (residues 107–132) binds to the SNX5 PX domain with a Kd of 0.9 µM.
source: Initial experiments with the human SNX5 and SNX6 PX domains showed robust interactions with the IncE C-terminal domain (residues 107–132). The affinities (Kd) for SNX5 and SNX6 were essentially indistinguishable (0.9 and 1.1 µM respectively)
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The C-terminal domain of IncE (residues 107–132) binds to the SNX6 PX domain with a Kd of 1.1 µM.
source: Initial experiments with the human SNX5 and SNX6 PX domains showed robust interactions with the IncE C-terminal domain (residues 107–132). The affinities (Kd) for SNX5 and SNX6 were essentially indistinguishable (0.9 and 1.1 µM respectively)
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: No interaction was detected between the IncE C-terminal domain and the PX domain of SNX1.
source: but we detected no interaction with the PX domain of SNX1 confirming the binding specificity.
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The PX domains of SNX5 and SNX6 possess a helix-turn-helix structural insert not found in any other SNX family members except for SNX32.
source: The PX domains of SNX5 and SNX6 possess a helix-turn-helix structural insert (Koharudin et al., 2009), which is not found in any other SNX family members except for SNX32 (Figure 2B)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Koharudin et al., 2009) and Figure 2B.

claim: SNX32 is a homologue expressed primarily in neurons.
source: a homologue expressed primarily in neurons (BioGPS (Wu et al., 2009)).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to BioGPS database (Wu et al., 2009).

claim: IncE binds to the SNX32 PX domain with a Kd of 1.0 µM.
source: Confirming a common recruitment motif in the SNX5-related proteins, ITC showed a strong interaction between IncE and the SNX32 PX domain similar to SNX5 and SNX6 (Kd = 1.0 µM) (Figure 2A; Table 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: SNX32 was robustly recruited to inclusion membranes in infected cells.
source: and SNX32 was robustly recruited to inclusion membranes in infected cells (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The shortest region of IncE able to support full binding to SNX5 encompasses residues 110–131 (GPAVQFFKGKNGSADQVILVT).
source: These experiments showed that the shortest region of IncE able to support full binding to SNX5 encompasses residues 110–131 (GPAVQFFKGKNGSADQVILVT)
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC truncation experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: A shorter IncE fragment containing residues 113–130 (VQFFKGKNGSADQVILV) can bind to SNX5 with a slightly reduced affinity.
source: while a shorter fragment containing residues 113–130 (VQFFKGKNGSADQVILV) can bind to SNX5 with a slightly reduced affinity.
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC truncation experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The SNX5-binding sequence of IncE appears to be preserved in all detected C. trachomatis variants.
source: While variations are observed across the different C. trachomatis serovars (Harris et al., 2012) the SNX5-binding sequence appears to be preserved in all detected variants (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3D and citation (Harris et al., 2012).

claim: IncE is clearly identifiable only in C. trachomatis, C. muridarum and C. suis.
source: A comparison with other chlamydial species suggests that IncE is not very widely conserved in this Genus, being clearly identifiable only in the closely related mouse pathogen C. muridarum and swine pathogen C. suis (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence comparison data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Residues required for binding to SNX5 are preserved in IncE homologues from C. muridarum and C. suis.
source: Residues required for binding to SNX5 are preserved in these IncE homologues
evidence: The claim is inferred from sequence alignment data.

claim: The canonical PX domain structure is composed of a three-stranded β-sheet (β1, β2 and β3) followed by three close-packed α-helices.
source: The canonical PX domain structure is composed of a three-stranded β-sheet (β1, β2 and β3) followed by three close-packed α-helices.
evidence: The claim is based on established structural knowledge of PX domains.

claim: SNX5, SNX6 and SNX32 possess major alterations in the PtdIns3P-binding pocket that preclude canonical lipid head-group docking.
source: In contrast SNX5, SNX6 and SNX32 possess major alterations in the PtdIns3P-binding pocket that preclude canonical lipid head-group docking (see below).
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: SNX5, SNX6 and SNX32 possess a unique extended helix-turn-helix insert between the Pro-rich loop and α2 helix.
source: In addition they possess a unique extended helix-turn-helix insert between the Pro-rich loop and α2 helix of unknown function (Figure 2B) (Koharudin et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation (Koharudin et al., 2009) and Figure 2B.

claim: The crystal structure of the SNX5-IncE complex was determined in three different spacegroups.
source: This construct readily crystallised in several crystal forms, and we were able to determine the structure of the complex in three different spacegroups (Figure 4; Table 3; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 4, Table 3, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The mode of IncE-binding to SNX5 is identical in all three crystal structures.
source: Confirming that the fusion does not alter complex formation, the short linker region is disordered, and the mode of IncE-binding to SNX5 is identical in all three structures (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The IncE sequence forms a long β-hairpin structure that binds within a complementary groove at the base of the extended α-helical insertion of the SNX5 PX domain.
source: The IncE sequence forms a long β-hairpin structure that binds within a complementary groove at the base of the extended α-helical insertion of the SNX5 PX domain and adjacent to the β-sheet sub-domain (Figure 4A; Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4A and Video 2.

claim: The β-hairpin structure of IncE is directly incorporated as a β-sheet augmentation of the β1, β2 and β3 strands of SNX5.
source: The β-hairpin structure of IncE (N-terminal βA and C-terminal βB strands) is directly incorporated as a β-sheet augmentation of the β1, β2 and β3 strands of SNX5 (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The N-terminal βA strand of the IncE sequence (Gly111-Lys118) forms the primary interface with SNX5.
source: The N-terminal βA strand of the IncE sequence (Gly111-Lys118) forms the primary interface with SNX5, making main-chain hydrogen bonds with the β1 strand of the SNX5 PX domain for the stable positioning of the IncE structure.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: SNX5 L133D and F136A mutations abolished association with the IncE peptide.
source: Because Leu133 and Phe136 residues in SNX5 are located at the core of the IncE-binding interface, and also due to the structural rearrangements these residues make on binding (see below), we reasoned that L133D and F136A mutations would inhibit the interaction. Indeed these mutants abolished association with the IncE peptide (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: IncE F116A and V127D mutations abolished binding to the SNX5 PX domain.
source: The reciprocal mutations in IncE residues F116A and V127D also abolished binding to the SNX5 PX domain (Figure 5B)
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: IncE F116A mutation abolished binding to SNX6 and SNX32 PX domains.
source: The reciprocal mutations in IncE residues F116A and V127D also abolished binding to the SNX5 PX domain (Figure 5B), and the SNX6 and SNX32 PX domains (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutations predicted to disrupt an observed electrostatic contact (IncE K118A or SNX5 E144A) had little effect on binding.
source: In contrast mutations predicted to disrupt an observed electrostatic contact (IncE K118A or SNX5 E144A) had little effect on binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: GFP-SNX5 protein showed clear and uniform recruitment to the limiting membrane of the inclusion.
source: Cells expressing the GFP-SNX5 protein showed clear and uniform recruitment to the limiting membrane of the inclusion as defined by mCherry-Rab25 (Figure 6A)
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The GFP-SNX5 (F136A) mutant protein showed no recruitment to the chlamydial inclusion.
source: In contrast, the GFP-SNX5 (F136A) mutant protein showed no recruitment to the chlamydial inclusion.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: GFP-SNX5 (F136A) mutant was able to co-immunoprecipitate endogenous SNX1 in heterodimeric complexes identically to the wild-type GFP-SNX5 protein.
source: Like wild-type GFP-SNX5 the GFP-SNX5 (F136A) mutant was recruited to punctate endosomal structures throughout the cytoplasm of these cells, and in addition was able to co-immunoprecipate endogenous SNX1 in heterodimeric complexes identically to the wild-type GFP-SNX5 protein (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Wild-type GFP-IncE(91-132) was recruited to endosomal structures via its interaction with SNX5-related proteins in both uninfected and infected HeLa cells.
source: The wild-type GFP-IncE(91-132) was recruited to endosomal structures via its interaction with SNX5-related proteins in both uninfected and infected HeLa cells (Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: GFP-IncE(91-132)(F116D), a SNX5-binding mutant, was exclusively cytosolic.
source: In contrast however, GFP-IncE(91-132)(F116D), a SNX5-binding mutant, was exclusively cytosolic.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Superposition of the SNX5-IncE complex with the SNX5 PX domain in the apo state reveals a significant conformational change in the α-helical extension.
source: Superposition of the SNX5-IncE complex with the SNX5 PX domain in the apo state (Koharudin et al., 2009) reveals a significant conformational change in the α-helical extension, as well as localized alterations in the loop between the β1 and β2 strands to accommodate peptide binding (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 7A and citation (Koharudin et al., 2009).

claim: The α-helical extension undergoes a maximal movement of ~8–10 Å at the furthest tip upon IncE binding.
source: Overall the α-helical extension undergoes a maximal movement of ~8–10 Å at the furthest tip, facilitated by the flexibility of the structure following the Pro-rich linker and an apparent hinge-point at Pro97 (Figure 7A upper panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The IncE peptide binds to a hydrophobic surface groove that is strictly conserved in the SNX5-related protein family.
source: Interestingly, when a cross-species evolutionary analysis of side-chain conservation in the SNX5-related proteins is performed it is clear that the IncE peptide binds a hydrophobic surface groove that is strictly conserved in this protein family (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by evolutionary conservation analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The high degree of conservation in the IncE binding surface of SNX5 implies that this site is normally engaged in a protein-protein interaction with an as yet unidentified binding partner(s).
source: This very strongly implies that the site is normally engaged in a protein-protein interaction with an as yet unidentified binding partner(s) required for SNX5's regular biological function, and that IncE is directly competing for this interface.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the evolutionary conservation data.

claim: IncE is directly competing for the conserved SNX5 binding interface.
source: This very strongly implies that the site is normally engaged in a protein-protein interaction with an as yet unidentified binding partner(s) required for SNX5's regular biological function, and that IncE is directly competing for this interface.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the evolutionary conservation data and structural analysis.

claim: More than fifty putative Incs have been identified in C. trachomatis.
source: Although more than fifty putative Incs have been identified in C. trachomatis, the exact roles of these inclusion membrane proteins are still poorly understood.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about chlamydial biology.

claim: This study presents the first reported crystal structure of a chlamydial inclusion protein (IncE) binding to its host effector protein (SNX5).
source: In this study, we present the first reported crystal structure of a chlamydial inclusion protein (IncE) binding to its host effector protein (SNX5).
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystallographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SNX1, SNX2, SNX5, SNX6 and the associated retromer complex have been directly implicated in the cellular pathogenesis of Coxiella burnetii.
source: In addition to C. trachomatis, SNX1, SNX2, SNX5, SNX6 and the associated retromer complex have also been directly implicated in the cellular pathogenesis of Coxiella burnetii (McDonough et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (McDonough et al., 2013).

claim: SNX1, SNX2, SNX5, SNX6 and the associated retromer complex have been directly implicated in the cellular pathogenesis of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium.
source: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (Bujny et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Bujny et al., 2008).

claim: SNX1, SNX2, SNX5, SNX6 and the associated retromer complex have been directly implicated in the cellular pathogenesis of hepatitis C virus.
source: hepatitis C virus (Yin et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Yin et al., 2016).

claim: SNX1, SNX2, SNX5, SNX6 and the associated retromer complex have been directly implicated in the cellular pathogenesis of human papilloma virus.
source: human papilloma virus (Ganti et al., 2016; Popa et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ganti et al., 2016; Popa et al., 2015).

claim: SNX1, SNX2, SNX5, SNX6 and the associated retromer complex have been directly implicated in the cellular pathogenesis of Legionella pneumophila.
source: and Legionella pneumophila (Finsel et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Finsel et al., 2013).

claim: PX domains of sorting nexins, including SNX1 and SNX2, play an important role in endosomal membrane recruitment by binding the endosome-enriched lipid PtdIns3P.
source: Typically PX domains of sorting nexins, including SNX1 and SNX2 (Cozier et al., 2002; Zhong et al., 2005), play an important role in endosomal membrane recruitment by binding the endosome-enriched lipid PtdIns3P through four conserved residues (Mas et al., 2014; Teasdale and Collins, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cozier et al., 2002; Zhong et al., 2005; Mas et al., 2014; Teasdale and Collins, 2012).

claim: The four conserved residues for PtdIns3P binding are conserved in most PX domains including in SNX1 and SNX2, but are entirely absent in SNX5, SNX6 and SNX32.
source: These residues are conserved in most PX domains including in SNX1 and SNX2, but are entirely absent in SNX5, SNX6 and SNX32.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence and structural analysis.

claim: There is evidence for the weak association of the SNX5 PX domain with the lipid PtdIns(4,5)P2 from NMR spectroscopy experiments.
source: Although there is evidence for the weak association of the SNX5 PX domain with the lipid PtdIns(4,5)P2 from nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy experiments (Koharudin et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Koharudin et al., 2009).

claim: The crystal structure does not point to a clear binding mechanism for PtdIns(4,5)P2 binding to SNX5.
source: the crystal structure does not point to a clear binding mechanism.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Expression of a GFP-tagged IncE C-terminal domain interfered with the SNX5/SNX6-dependent retrograde trafficking of the cation-independent mannose-6-phosphate receptor (CI-MPR).
source: Previously, the expression of a GFP-tagged IncE C-terminal domain was shown to interfere with the SNX5/SNX6-dependent retrograde trafficking of the cation-independent mannose-6-phosphate receptor (CI-MPR) (Mirrashidi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Mirrashidi et al., 2015).

claim: IncE is mimicking and interfering with SNX5/SNX6-mediated protein interactions with a ligand(s) required for normal endosomal trafficking.
source: Combined with our structural data, this infers that IncE is mimicking and interfering with SNX5/SNX6-mediated protein interactions, with a ligand(s) required for normal endosomal trafficking that remains to be discovered.
evidence: The claim is inferred from structural data and previous functional studies.

claim: Knockdown of SNX5 and SNX6 results in an increased production of C. trachomatis infectious progeny.
source: While it is logical to imagine they could play a positive role in the sculpting of the inclusion, this is somewhat difficult to reconcile with the effect of SNX5 and SNX6 knockdown, which results in an increased production of C. trachomatis infectious progeny.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The role of IncE could be to compete for SNX-retromer endosomal interactions, resulting in the breakdown of normal trafficking of the CI-MPR and lysosomal hydrolases.
source: It was thus proposed that the role of IncE could be to compete for SNX-retromer endosomal interactions, resulting in the breakdown of normal trafficking of the CI-MPR and lysosomal hydrolases and hence perturbation of the endolysosomal system's capacity for bacterial destruction (Aeberhard et al., 2015; Mirrashidi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is a proposed hypothesis supported by citations (Aeberhard et al., 2015; Mirrashidi et al., 2015).

claim: SNX recruitment to the inclusion occurs via protein-protein interactions and does not depend on the presence of 3-phosphoinositide lipids.
source: This offers two possibilities; that either SNX recruitment to the inclusion occurs via protein-protein interactions, and does not depend on the presence of 3-phosphoinositide lipids that typically recruit SNX proteins to endosomal membranes, or alternatively that PI3Ks are not present at the inclusion and therefore wortmannin treatment has no effect at this particular compartment. Given our structural and mutagenesis studies below we favor the former explanation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from wortmannin treatment experiments and structural/mutagenesis data.

claim: A common structure within the SNX5, SNX6 and SNX32 PX domains is required for IncE interaction.
source: Overall, our data indicates that a common structure within the SNX5, SNX6 and SNX32 PX domains is required for IncE interaction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from ITC binding data and structural analysis.

claim: BAR-domain mediated heterodimer formation with SNX1 or SNX2 is required for endosomal recruitment of SNX5.
source: This implies that BAR-domain mediated heterodimer formation with SNX1 or SNX2 is required for endosomal recruitment, and is not perturbed by the IncE-binding mutation in the PX domain.
evidence: The claim is inferred from co-immunoprecipitation and localization data.

claim: Val114 of IncE inserts into a pocket formed primarily by Tyr132 and Phe136 on the SNX5 α'' helix.
source: At the N-terminus of the βA strand Val114 of IncE inserts into a pocket formed primarily by Tyr132 and Phe136 on the SNX5 α'' helix (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: IncE Phe116 makes π-stacking with the Phe136 side-chain and hydrophobic docking with Val140 of SNX5.
source: A major contribution comes from IncE Phe116, with π-stacking occurring with the Phe136 side-chain and hydrophobic docking with Val140 of SNX5 (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: IncE Lys118 makes an electrostatic contact with SNX5 Glu144.
source: Adjacent to IncE Phe116 at the end of the βA strand Lys118 makes an electrostatic contact with SNX5 Glu144.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis.

claim: IncE Val127 and Leu129 contact an extended SNX5 surface composed of Leu133, Tyr132 and Met106.
source: Finally, at the C-terminal end of the IncE βB strand Val127 and Leu129 contact an extended SNX5 surface composed of Leu133, Tyr132 and Met106 (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The core hydrophobic interactions are critical for IncE binding but the peripheral electrostatic contact is not essential.
source: Thus the core hydrophobic interactions are critical for IncE binding but the peripheral electrostatic contact is not essential.
evidence: The claim is inferred from mutagenesis data.

claim: SNX5-related proteins are directly associated with the inclusion via IncE protein-protein interactions in a phosphoinositide-independent manner.
source: We propose that in the context of C. trachomatis infection, SNX5-related proteins are directly associated with the inclusion via IncE protein-protein interactions in a phosphoinositide-independent manner
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on structural and experimental data.

claim: SNX5-related proteins are able to recruit their heterodimeric partners SNX1 and SNX2.
source: and are able to recruit their heterodimeric partners SNX1 and SNX2 (Sierecki et al., 2014; van Weering et al., 2012; Wassmer et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Sierecki et al., 2014; van Weering et al., 2012; Wassmer et al., 2009).

claim: The PX-BAR-domain containing complexes are localised to the inclusion in a retromer-independent manner.
source: The PX-BAR-domain containing complexes are then localised to the inclusion in a retromer-independent manner (Mirrashidi et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Mirrashidi et al., 2015).

claim: The IncE sequence used in this study is from the L3 serovar L3/404/LN (NCBI reference WP_015506602).
source: The IncE sequence used in this study is from the L3 serovar L3/404/LN (NCBI reference WP_015506602) (Harris et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is a methodological statement supported by citation (Harris et al., 2012).

claim: The first three IncE N-terminal residues (Pro107, Ala108, Asn109) and the last three IncE C-terminal residues (Val130, Thr131, Gln132) were not modeled due to lack of electron density.
source: The first three IncE N-terminal residues (Pro107, Ala108, Asn109) and the last three IncE C-terminal residues (Val130, Thr131, Gln132) were not modeled due to lack of electron density, suggesting disorder and matching precisely with our mapping experiments showing these residues are not necessary for SNX5 association.
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data and ITC mapping experiments.

claim: The two anti-parallel β-strands of IncE are connected by a short loop (Gly119-Ala124) that makes no direct contact with the SNX5 protein.
source: The two anti-parallel β-strands of IncE are connected by a short loop (Gly119-Ala124) that makes no direct contact with the SNX5 protein
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis.

claim: The C-terminal IncE βB strand (Asp125-Val130) forms an interface with the extended α-helical region of the SNX5 PX domain.
source: and the C-terminal IncE βB strand (Asp125-Val130) forms an interface with the extended α-helical region of the SNX5 PX domain.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis.
